title: The Expert Equation
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart lays out several distinctions between novices and experts, surface versus deep structure recognition, naming versus functional understanding, basic versus genuine knowledge creation, and need for scaffolding versus independent critical thinking, and then proposes what he calls the Expert Equation: Knowledge times Effective Practice times Time equals Degree of Expertise. He uses the multiplicative structure to argue that a deficiency in any one factor caps growth regardless of strength in the others; insufficient knowledge limits what practice can accomplish, ineffective practice wastes time even with strong knowledge, and inconsistent opportunity blocks progress even when knowledge and practice quality are both good. He translates this into a concrete instructional prompt: for any given lesson, ask what percentage of it provides students a real opportunity to both gain knowledge and practice using it effectively, and treat that percentage as a lever for accelerating growth toward expertise.
points: The Expert Equation, Knowledge times Effective Practice times Time equals Degree of Expertise, is explicitly multiplicative in Stuart's framing, meaning a weak factor constrains overall growth even when the other two are strong.
Novices are distinguished from experts along several axes: surface versus deep structure, naming versus functional understanding, and dependence on scaffolding versus independent critical thinking.

Practical instructional question: what percentage of a given lesson actually provides students the chance to both gain knowledge and practice using it, treating that percentage itself as an improvable target.

Knowledge-rich, practice-dense lessons repeated lesson after lesson, year after year are positioned as the mechanism by which K-12 education moves students meaningfully toward expertise, not any single high-impact activity.
quotes: Novices tend to see the superficial aspects of a problem or text, whereas experts see the problem's deeper structure.

Novice musicians learn to play music; expert musicians are capable of composing music. Novice historians learn the facts of history; expert historians are capable of creating history through analyzing primary sources.

If students don't know enough in a given discipline, no amount of practice or time will get them closer to expertise. We think with what we know. This is an inescapable reality of the human learning system.
If students know a lot but aren't taught how to effectively use (i.e., practice with) that knowledge, no amount of time will get them closer to expertise. Not all types of practice are equal.

To help students acquire as much mastery (i.e., as much movement towards expertise) as possible in a K-12 education, they need knowledge-rich learning experiences filled with effective practice, lesson after lesson, year after year.

If only 50% of your lessons do these things or you do these things with only 50% of your allotted lesson time, your students will grow to a significantly lesser degree than if you moved those percentages up to 60% or 70% or 80%.
